dedupe_keys.name: southeastern liberia mapping remote communities from satellite images to plan community health services

description: This case study tests whether deep learning on satellite images can map where people live in remote areas so that community health systems can plan and deliver services. The authors, from the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, the University of Washington and Boston College, trained an algorithm to detect individual buildings and then grouped building clusters into probable communities, and validated the results in southeastern Liberia against community locations recorded by enumerators and community health workers. The article was published in 2019 in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, and an author version is free to read online in PubMed Central. Coverage is a rural region of Liberia. Caveats: satellite detection finds buildings, not people, and the enumeration data and model are not stated to be public. Building detection reached a positive predictive value of 86.47 percent and a sensitivity of 79.49 percent; the method found 75.67 percent (451) of the communities registered by enumeration and 167 potential communities not previously registered, with some false positives and negatives. The authors conclude that satellite analysis is a rapid, low-cost way to map remote communities, pending checks on the unregistered finds. Simulation uses: settlement locations for health service catchment, outreach routing and access models in data-poor regions. Related records: the Liberia national EMS study (case_study-liberia-national-ems-first-22-months) and the LISGIS census data (data-lisgis-liberia-open-data-api-census-2022-household-deprivation-electricity-water-sanitation-floor-cooking-by-county) describe related Liberian services and population.
